normalization_notes: Prices are Linux, pay-as-you-go list prices in US dollars, excluding tax, discounts, commitments, spot capacity and free tiers.
Hourly prices are multiplied by hours_per_month. Where a provider publishes a monthly price or cap, the lower of the two is used.

Each provider lists general-purpose virtual servers from 1 to 64 vCPUs: its shared or burstable line and its general, compute and memory lines, in the newest two generations it sells. GPU, storage-optimised, bare-metal and other specialist families are left out.
memory_gb is the provider’s own figure. The large clouds quote GiB; the difference from GB is ignored.
cpu and cpu_launch_year record what the provider documents about the processor. Null means the provider does not say, or the family runs on a mix of generations.
recent_cpu_since is the launch year used by the widget’s recent-processor option: a family qualifies only if its documented processor generation launched in that year or later.

cpu_share marks families that are not a full-time dedicated processor: burstable (credit based), shared (processor time shared with other customers) or flex (AWS, full performance at least 95% of the time).

Disk classes describe performance as a base figure, a floor, growth per GB and a maximum. A class with a provision block lets IOPS and throughput be bought separately above the free base; a class with size_tiers is sold only in fixed sizes.
performance_target is what the high-performance disk option provisions. disk_fast lists the classes a provider or family may use to reach it; the widget picks the cheapest that can.
Data transfer, public IP addresses, backups, snapshots and licences are not included.

providers.name: AWS EC2
notes: A public IPv4 address is charged separately at $0.005 an hour.
Burstable T instances run in unlimited mode by default, so sustained CPU use above the baseline is billed extra.
The io2 Block Express class costs more than gp3 at the performance target used here, so gp3 with provisioned IOPS is used for the high-performance option.

t3.cpu: Intel Xeon Scalable 1st or 2nd gen (Skylake or Cascade Lake)

providers.name: Azure Virtual Machines
providers.billing: per minute: prices are quoted per hour and you are charged for the whole minutes a VM runs; a trailing part-minute is not billed
notes: Standard SSD also bills $0.002 per 10,000 disk transactions, which is not included.
The B-series v1 and Fsv2 families are left out because new subscriptions can no longer deploy them.
Intel v7 sizes are listed for East US only; Microsoft has not announced them for UK South or West Europe.

providers.name: Google Compute Engine
notes: The N4 and C4 families accept only Hyperdisk; E2, N2, N2D, T2D and T2A accept only persistent disk. C3 and C3D accept both.

Hyperdisk Balanced is priced here at its free baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 140 MB/s unless the high-performance option is on. A volume created without explicit values is given more than that and billed for it.
Shared-core E2 sizes present 2 vCPUs but are entitled to a quarter, half or one vCPU of sustained use.

providers.name: DigitalOcean
providers.billing: per second, minimum charge 60 seconds or $0.01 if higher
notes: Monthly prices are a cap reached after 672 hours, so a full month costs less than the hourly rate times 730.
Volumes deliver 7,500 IOPS on shared-CPU Droplets and 10,000 IOPS on dedicated-CPU Droplets, at the same price.
The newer v5 Droplets are sold only in four US datacentres and are not included.
